tool.name: Kotlin
tool.tagline: Concise, null-safe JVM language for Android, backends and multiplatform apps
tool.description: Kotlin is a modern statically typed language from JetBrains that runs on the JVM, compiles to JavaScript and native code, and interoperates fully with Java. It is Google's preferred language for Android and widely used for server-side development with Spring and Ktor. Learning it gives you null safety, concise syntax, powerful functional features and coroutines for structured concurrency.

glossary.def: Java Virtual Machine: the program that runs compiled bytecode. Kotlin usually compiles for it, so Kotlin programs run wherever a JVM does and can use Java libraries.
The build tool most Kotlin projects use. Its script (build.gradle.kts, itself written in Kotlin) says how to compile, test and package the project and which libraries to download.
Kotlin's way of compiling the same code for several targets: the JVM, web browsers (JavaScript or WebAssembly) and native apps for iOS, desktop and servers.
Can be read but not changed through this name. A read-only list has no add or remove, though another part of the program holding it as mutable might still change it.
Kotlin's way of putting values into text: "Hi, $name" inserts a variable, and "${a + b}" inserts the result of an expression.
A run of values from a start to an end, such as 1..5 (1 to 5 inclusive) or 0 until 5 (0 to 4). Used in for loops and in checks like x in 1..10.
A when is exhaustive when it has a branch for every possible value, so the compiler can prove that nothing is missed.
A name followed by @ (such as outer@) placed on a loop or lambda, so that break@outer, continue@outer or return@forEach can say which one they mean.
Kotlin's type for 'no useful result', such as a function that only prints. You rarely have to write it.
The crash that happens when code uses a missing (null) value as if it were real. Kotlin's null safety prevents most of them.
Kotlin's system of marking which values may be null (String?) and checking before the program runs that you handle them, which prevents most NullPointerExceptions.
Kotlin's ?. operator: a?.b uses b only if a isn't null, and gives null otherwise.
Kotlin's ?: operator: a ?: b gives a if it isn't null, otherwise b. Named after its resemblance to Elvis Presley's hairstyle.
After a check such as if (x != null) or if (x is String), Kotlin automatically treats x as the narrower type inside that branch.
Kotlin's !! operator: it insists a value isn't null and throws a NullPointerException if it is.
A Kotlin modifier for a non-null var that gets its value after the object is created; reading it before that throws an error.
An object that holds a group of values. In Kotlin these are mainly lists, sets and maps, each in a read-only and a mutable version.
The brackets right after a Kotlin class name, listing the inputs needed to create an object; inputs marked val or var become properties.
A keyword (public, private, protected or internal) that controls which other code may use a class or member.
In Kotlin, a class marked data: from the properties in its primary constructor, Kotlin generates equals, hashCode, toString, copy and destructuring.
A method every object has that returns a number summarising its contents. Sets and maps use it to find items quickly; equal objects must return equal numbers.
To unpack an object's parts into separate variables in one step, as in val (name, age) = user.
A type describing a function's inputs and result, written like (Int, Int) -> Int. A variable of this type can hold any matching function or lambda.
Kotlin's rule that when a function's last parameter is a function, the lambda can be written after the closing bracket: repeat(3) { ... }.
A way to pass an existing function as a value with ::, such as ::isEven or String::length.
When a lambda uses a variable from the code around it, it captures that variable; in Kotlin it can even change a captured var.
In Kotlin, a lazily evaluated chain (made with asSequence() or sequence { }) that handles items one at a time and only as needed, instead of building a full list at each step.
An object declared inside a Kotlin class whose members belong to the class itself, called as ClassName.member; Kotlin's replacement for static.
Kotlin's object Name { } syntax, which defines a class and its single instance at once (a singleton).
Kotlin's object : SomeType { } syntax, which creates a one-off object of an unnamed class right where it is written.
A tag starting with @, such as @JvmStatic or @Test, attached to code. It adds information that the compiler or a framework reads.
A class or interface whose possible subclasses are all known when compiling, so a when over it can be checked to cover every case.
A function added to an existing type from outside it, written fun String.shout() = ...; it is called with a dot as if it were a member.
The object a function is called on: in "abc".uppercase(), "abc" is the receiver. Inside an extension function or lambda with receiver, this refers to it.
One of Kotlin's let, run, with, apply and also: functions that run a block of code with an object as it or this, returning the block's result or the object.
An exception that Java forces calling code to catch or declare. Kotlin has no checked exceptions, so you never have to.
The rules for when Box<Cat> may be used as Box<Animal>. Covariant (out) types only hand values out, contravariant (in) types only take them in, invariant types allow neither.
On the JVM, generic type arguments are removed after compiling, so while running a List<String> is just a List.
A type parameter of an inline function marked reified, whose actual type is kept at the call site, so code like x is T works.
Kotlin's List<*>: a list of some unknown type. You can read items as Any? but can't add any.
Kotlin's suspend functions can pause (suspend) at a call such as delay() without blocking their thread, and resume later; each such pause is a suspension point.
The rule that every coroutine runs inside a scope that waits for all its children and cancels them together, so no work is leaked or forgotten.
In Kotlin coroutines, the object that decides which threads run a coroutine, such as Dispatchers.Default, Dispatchers.IO or Dispatchers.Main.
A Kotlin coroutine stream that hands out many values over time, one by one, to whoever collects it.
A cold Flow runs its code anew for each collector, only when collected; a hot flow (StateFlow, SharedFlow) produces values whether or not anyone is listening.
An operation such as collect, toList or first that actually runs a Kotlin flow and gathers its values.
Kotlin's hot flows: a StateFlow always holds one current value and tells collectors about changes; a SharedFlow broadcasts events to everyone listening.
To hand a job to another object. In Kotlin, class delegation (by) forwards an interface's methods, and a delegated property hands its get and set to a helper such as lazy.
A type coming from Java code, shown as String!, whose nullability Kotlin doesn't know; you decide whether to treat it as nullable.
Passing a Kotlin lambda where an interface with a single abstract method (SAM) is expected, such as Java's Runnable or Comparator.
A method or field that belongs to a class itself rather than to one object. Java has them; Kotlin uses top-level functions and companion objects instead.
Kotlin's inline functions are copied, together with the lambdas passed to them, into every place that calls them, so no lambda object has to be created.
A bare return inside a lambda passed to an inline function, which returns from the surrounding function rather than just from the lambda.
A Kotlin class wrapping a single value (@JvmInline value class UserId(val raw: Long)) that is a distinct type to the compiler but usually stored as the bare value.
Wrapping a simple value, such as a number, in a full object so it can go where only objects are allowed. It costs memory and time.
When the compiler changes a function's name in the compiled output, for example adding a suffix, so that two versions can't clash.
A lambda of a type like StringBuilder.() -> Unit: inside it, this is the receiver, so its members can be called directly.
A Kotlin DSL made of functions that take lambdas with receivers, so nested blocks like html { body { } } build objects and are still checked by the compiler.
An object standing for 'the rest of the computation' after a pause. Kotlin compiles suspend functions to take a hidden continuation, which is called when the result is ready.
A function with one parameter marked infix, so it can be called without a dot or brackets, like a to b or 2 times 3.
A named value that never changes. In Kotlin, const val MAX = 10 declares one whose value is fixed when the program is compiled.
One of the alternative paths in an if/else or a when. Only the branch whose condition matches runs.
Kotlin's * in front of an array when calling a vararg function, as in sum(*numbers): it passes the array's items as separate arguments.
A property with a custom get() that works out its value each time it is read, instead of storing it.

concepts.name: Hello Kotlin: main and tooling
concepts.summary: Write your first Kotlin program around a main function, and learn how the compiler, the JVM, IntelliJ IDEA and Gradle fit together.
concepts.why: Getting a program running is the first step, and knowing what each tool does saves hours of confusion later.
concepts.body:
A program is a list of instructions for a computer. You write those instructions as text in files, and that text is called **source code**. Kotlin source files end in `.kt`. Here is a complete Kotlin program:

```kotlin
fun main() {
    println("Hello, Kotlin!")
}
```

`fun main()` defines a **function** named `main`: a named block of instructions. Every Kotlin program starts by running `main`. The curly braces `{ }` hold the function's body, and the instructions inside run from top to bottom. Each instruction is a **statement**; Kotlin needs no semicolon at the end of a line.

`println("Hello, Kotlin!")` calls the built-in function `println`, which prints the text in quotation marks and then starts a new line (`print` stays on the same line). A value you hand to a function in its brackets is an **argument**. Kotlin is **case-sensitive**: `println` works, `Println` doesn't.

Before it runs, your code is checked and translated by the **compiler**; this step is called *compiling*. If the compiler finds a mistake, it stops with a **compile error** that names the file and line.

Kotlin's compiler usually produces **bytecode**, which runs on the **JVM** (Java Virtual Machine): a program available for Windows, macOS and Linux. Java, an older language, runs on the JVM too, so Kotlin can use the huge number of Java **libraries**: ready-made code that others have written. Kotlin can also run in web browsers and as native apps (Kotlin Multiplatform).

Ways to run Kotlin:

- The online Kotlin Playground in your browser: nothing to install, ideal for first steps.
- An **IDE**, a program for writing code, such as IntelliJ IDEA (made by JetBrains, Kotlin's creator) or Android Studio: click the green run arrow next to `main`.
- **Gradle**, the **build tool** real projects use to compile, test and bundle everything: `./gradlew run`.
- The `kotlinc` compiler, typed in a **terminal** (a window for typing commands): `kotlinc hello.kt -include-runtime -d hello.jar`, then `java -jar hello.jar`.

To read a line the user types, call `readln()`. Words typed after the program's name arrive in `args` if you write `fun main(args: Array<String>)`.
takeaways: Every program starts at `fun main()`
The compiler turns `.kt` files into bytecode that the JVM runs
Experiment in the Kotlin Playground or IntelliJ IDEA; real projects build with Gradle
pitfalls: Writing `Println` or `Main`: Kotlin is case-sensitive, so the names must match exactly.

quiz.q: Where does a Kotlin program start running?
options: At the first line of the file
At the last function in the file
At whichever line the IDE cursor is on
quiz.explain: Kotlin looks for the function called main and runs it first; everything else is called from there.

concepts.name: val, var and basic types
concepts.summary: Store values in read-only val and changeable var variables, let Kotlin infer types, and use its number, true/false, character and text types.
concepts.why: Every program keeps values in variables, and choosing val and the right type up front makes Kotlin code safe and easy to follow.
concepts.body:
A **variable** is a name that holds a value so you can use it later. Kotlin has two kinds:

```kotlin
val name = "Ada"   // val: can't be given a new value
var age = 36       // var: can change
age = age + 1      // now 37
```

Text after `//` is a comment: a note for humans that the compiler ignores.

- `val` is **read-only**: once set, it can't be reassigned. Use it by default.
- `var` can be reassigned. Something that can be changed is called **mutable**. Use `var` only when the value really has to change.

Every value has a type that says what kind of value it is: `Int` for whole numbers, `String` for text. Usually Kotlin works the type out from the starting value; this is **type inference**. You can also write it after a colon: `val ratio: Double = 0.5`. Whichever you choose, the type is fixed: the compiler rejects `age = "old"` before the program runs. That makes Kotlin **statically typed**.

The basic types:

- Whole numbers: `Int` (the default, up to about ±2.1 billion) and `Long` for bigger ones (`3L`). `Byte`, `Short` and unsigned `UInt`, `ULong` exist too.
- Numbers with decimals: `Double` (the default, as in `9.99`) and the less precise `Float` (`1.5f`). These are **floating-point numbers**, stored approximately.
- `Boolean` for `true` or `false` (a **boolean** value), `Char` for one character (`'a'`), and `String` for text.

A value written straight into code, like `42` or `"Ada"`, is a **literal**. Underscores make big numbers readable: `1_000_000`.

Kotlin never converts between number types on its own: an `Int` can't go into a `Long` variable without `toLong()`. Use `toInt()`, `toDouble()` and friends. Arithmetic works as at school, except that dividing two whole numbers drops the remainder, which is called **integer division**: `7 / 2` is `3`, while `7 / 2.0` is `3.5`. `%` gives the remainder.

`const val MAX_USERS = 100` at the top of a file declares a **constant**, a value fixed when the program is compiled.

One subtlety: `val` stops the name from pointing at something else, not the thing itself from changing. A `val list = mutableListOf(1)` can still get new items with `list.add(2)`; lists come in a later lesson.
concepts.code:
const val MAX_USERS = 100

fun main() {
    val name = "Ada"            // String, read-only
    var age = 36                // Int, can change
    age += 1                    // same as age = age + 1
    val big: Long = 3_000_000_000
    val ratio = 7 / 2           // integer division: 3
    val exact = 7 / 2.0         // Double: 3.5
    println("$name $age $ratio $exact")   // Ada 37 3 3.5

    val i = 42
    val l: Long = i.toLong()    // no automatic conversion
    println(l + big)            // 3000000042
    println(MAX_USERS.coerceAtMost(50))   // 50

    val list = mutableListOf(1)
    list.add(2)                 // the val can't be reassigned, but the list can grow
    println(list)               // [1, 2]
}
takeaways: Use `val` by default, `var` only when the value must change
Types are inferred, but fixed before the program runs
No automatic number conversion: call `toLong()`, `toDouble()`...
`val` stops reassignment, not changes inside a list
pitfalls: Assuming `val list = mutableListOf()` can never change: its contents still can.

quiz.q: Which line compiles? (x is an Int)
quiz.explain: Kotlin never converts between number types by itself, so you must call toLong().

concepts.name: Strings and templates
concepts.summary: Work with text: put values into strings with string templates, write multi-line raw strings, and use the common String functions.
concepts.why: Text is everywhere (what users type, what you print, what you save) and Kotlin's string templates make it concise and readable.
concepts.body:
In programming, a piece of text is called a **string**: a string of characters. In Kotlin its type is `String`, and you write it in double quotation marks: `"Ada"`. A string never changes once created; it is **immutable**. Functions like `uppercase()` give you a *new* string and leave the original alone.

**String templates** put values into text. `"Hello, $name"` inserts a variable, and `"Total: ${price * qty}"` inserts the result of any **expression**, a piece of code that works out to a value. That is tidier than joining pieces with `+`, which is called **concatenation**, though that works too.

**Raw strings** start and end with three quotation marks. They can span several lines and contain `"` and `\` characters just as they are, which suits text such as a letter or a snippet of data. Call `trimIndent()` to remove the indentation shared by all lines. (From Kotlin 2.2 you can start a string with `$$` when the text itself is full of `$` signs; then only `$$name` inserts a value.)

Strings have many functions you call with a dot:

- `length` (the number of characters), `uppercase()`, `lowercase()`, `trim()` (removes spaces at both ends), `padStart(5, '0')`.
- `contains`, `startsWith`, `endsWith`, `indexOf`, `substring`, `replace`.
- `split(",")` cuts the text into pieces; `lines()` splits it into lines.
- `s[0]` is the first character (positions count from 0), plus `first()`, `last()`, `take(3)`, `drop(1)`.
- `isBlank()` (empty or only spaces) and `isNotEmpty()`.

Turning text into a number is called **parsing**: `"42".toInt()` gives 42. If the text isn't a number, `toInt()` stops the program with an error, while `toIntOrNull()` gives **null**, Kotlin's word for "no value" (the Null safety lesson covers it).

Compare text with `==`, which compares the characters. (`===` asks whether two names refer to the very same stored copy, which you rarely want for strings.)

When you add to text many times, for example inside a loop (code that repeats, coming up next), use `buildString { append(...) }`. `"%.2f".format(x)` shows a number with two decimals.
concepts.code:
fun main() {
    val name = "Ada"
    val items = listOf("pen", "ink")           // a list of two strings (lists come later)
    println("Hello, $name! You have ${items.size} items.") // Hello, Ada! You have 2 items.

    val note = """
        Dear $name,
        see you "soon".
    """.trimIndent()
    println(note)                              // Dear Ada, / see you "soon".

    println("  hi  ".trim().uppercase())       // HI
    println("7".padStart(3, '0'))              // 007
    println("12x".toIntOrNull())               // null
    println("a,b,c".split(","))                // [a, b, c]
    println("%.2f".format(3.14159))            // 3.14

    val report = buildString {
        for (i in 1..3) append(i).append(';')  // repeats for i = 1, 2, 3
    }
    println(report)                            // 1;2;3;
}
takeaways: `$name` and `${expr}` put values into text
Triple-quoted raw strings with `trimIndent()` for multi-line text
`==` compares the characters of two strings
Use `toIntOrNull()` to parse text safely
pitfalls: Calling `name.uppercase()` on its own line and expecting `name` to change: strings never change, so keep the result.

quiz.q: What does "Sum: ${1 + 2}" evaluate to?
quiz.explain: ${...} evaluates the expression inside and inserts its value.

concepts.name: if, when and loops
concepts.summary: Make decisions with if and when, which both produce values, and repeat work with for loops over ranges and with while.
concepts.why: Every program makes decisions and repeats work; in Kotlin, if and when even hand back values, replacing a lot of clumsy code.
concepts.body:
Programs need to make decisions. A **conditional** runs code only when a condition is true:

```kotlin
if (temperature > 25) {
    println("Warm")
} else {
    println("Cool")
}
```

The condition must be a **boolean**, `true` or `false`. You build conditions with comparison **operators**: `==` (equal), `!=` (not equal), `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`. Combine them with `&&` (and), `||` (or) and `!` (not).

In Kotlin, `if` is an **expression**: a piece of code that produces a value. So `val max = if (a > b) a else b` stores the bigger number.

`when` chooses between many options and is also an expression:

```kotlin
val label = when (code) {
    200, 204 -> "ok"
    in 400..499 -> "client error"
    else -> "other"
}
```

Each option is a **branch**. Branches can match several values (`200, 204`), a **range** of numbers (`in 400..499`), a type (`is String`), or, with nothing after `when`, any condition (`when { x < 0 -> ... }`). Only the first matching branch runs. A `when` that produces a value must be **exhaustive**, covering every possibility, usually by ending with `else`.

A **loop** repeats code, and each pass is one **iteration**:

- `for (i in 1..5)` counts from 1 to 5 (`..` includes the end). `0 until n` and `0..<n` stop just before `n`; `10 downTo 0 step 2` counts down in twos.
- `for (ch in "abc")` visits each character; the same works for lists.
- `while (cond) { ... }` repeats as long as the condition stays true. `do { ... } while (cond)` checks at the end, so the body always runs at least once.

`break` leaves a loop and `continue` jumps to its next iteration. To leave an outer loop from inside an inner one, give the outer loop a **label**: `outer@ for (...)`, then `break@outer`.

Later lessons show functions like `forEach`, `map` and `filter` that replace many loops; a `for` loop stays the clearest choice when you need to stop early.
takeaways: `if` and `when` are expressions that produce values
`when` matches values, ranges, types or conditions; only the first match runs
`1..n` includes n; `until` and `..<` stop before it
`break@outer` leaves an outer loop from an inner one
pitfalls: Forgetting `else` in a `when` that produces a value from an `Int`: it doesn't cover every case, so it won't compile.

quiz.q: What does for (i in 0 until 3) iterate over?
quiz.explain: until excludes the upper bound.

concepts.name: Functions
concepts.summary: Write your own functions with typed parameters, default and named arguments, one-line bodies and any number of arguments.
concepts.why: Functions let you name an idea once and reuse it, and Kotlin's default and named arguments keep calls short and clear.
concepts.body:
A function is a named block of code you can run, or *call*, whenever you need it. You've been calling `println`; here is how to write your own:

```kotlin
fun add(a: Int, b: Int): Int {
    return a + b
}
```

Read it left to right: `fun`, the name, the **parameters** in brackets (named inputs, each with a type), then a colon and the type of the result. `return` hands back the result, the **return value**. Calling `add(2, 3)` passes the arguments 2 and 3 and gives back 5.

When the body is a single expression (one piece of code that works out to a value), drop the braces and `return`: `fun add(a: Int, b: Int) = a + b`. A function with no useful result returns `Unit` ("nothing"), which you don't need to write.

Parameter features:

- **Default values**: `fun greet(name: String, greeting: String = "Hello")`. Callers may leave `greeting` out, so one function covers several ways of calling it.
- **Named arguments**: `greet(name = "Ada", greeting = "Hi")` makes calls easy to read and lets you skip defaults or give arguments in any order.
- `vararg` accepts any number of arguments: `fun sum(vararg xs: Int)`. To pass an existing array (a fixed group of values), put the **spread operator** `*` in front of it: `sum(*arr)`.
- Parameters are read-only, like `val`.

Functions can sit at the **top level** of a file, outside everything else, or inside another function as a **local function** that hides a small helper.

**Infix functions** read like words between two values: the built-in `to` makes a pair, `"a" to 1`.

To give back two results, return a `Pair` and unpack it into two variables: `val (low, high) = minMax(numbers)`. Unpacking like this is called **destructuring**. For more than two results, a data class (covered later) reads better.
concepts.code:
fun add(a: Int, b: Int) = a + b

fun greet(name: String, greeting: String = "Hello", punct: String = "!") =
    "$greeting, $name$punct"

fun sum(vararg xs: Int): Int = xs.sum()

fun minMax(xs: List<Int>): Pair<Int, Int> = xs.min() to xs.max()   // List<Int>: a list of whole numbers

fun main() {
    println(add(2, 3))                          // 5
    println(greet("Ada"))                       // Hello, Ada!
    println(greet("Ada", punct = "?"))          // Hello, Ada?
    println(greet(greeting = "Hi", name = "Bo"))// Hi, Bo!
    println(sum(1, 2, 3))                       // 6
    val arr = intArrayOf(4, 5)
    println(sum(*arr))                          // 9
    val (lo, hi) = minMax(listOf(4, 9, 1))
    println("$lo..$hi")                         // 1..9

    fun square(x: Int) = x * x                  // local function
    println(square(7))                          // 49
}
takeaways: `fun name(p: Type): Result`; one-line bodies use `=`
Default and named arguments let one function serve many kinds of call
Functions can live at the top level of a file
Return a `Pair` (or a data class) and destructure it
pitfalls: Mixing up the order of several arguments of the same type: use named arguments, such as `greet(name = "Ada", greeting = "Hi")`.

quiz.q: Given fun f(a: Int = 1, b: Int = 2) = a * 10 + b, what is f(b = 5)?
quiz.explain: a keeps its default 1 and b is 5, so 1 * 10 + 5 = 15.

concepts.name: Null safety
concepts.summary: Handle missing values safely with nullable types, safe calls, the Elvis operator and smart casts, and avoid the crash-prone !!.
concepts.why: Null safety is Kotlin's signature feature: it removes the most common crash in programming, and it shapes every Kotlin program you read.
concepts.body:
Sometimes a value is missing: a user has no middle name, a search finds nothing. Kotlin represents "no value" with null. In many languages any variable can secretly hold null, and using it crashes the program with an error called a **NullPointerException**. Kotlin's **null safety** prevents that before the program runs.

By default a type can't hold null: a `String` variable always holds real text. To allow null, add `?`. A `String?` holds text or null; such a type is **nullable**.

You can't use a nullable value directly: `name.length` doesn't compile when `name` is a `String?`. Instead:

- **Safe call** `name?.length` gives the length, or null if `name` is null. Calls can chain: `user?.address?.city`.
- **Elvis operator** `?:` supplies a fallback: `name?.length ?: 0`. The right side can even be `return`, to leave a function early.
- **Smart cast**: after a check like `if (name != null)`, the compiler lets you use `name` as a plain `String` inside that branch.
- `name?.let { ... }` runs the code in braces only when `name` isn't null; inside, the value is called `it`.
- **Not-null assertion** `name!!` means "trust me, it isn't null", and crashes with a NullPointerException if you're wrong. Treat every `!!` as a warning sign.

Helpers that give null instead of failing: `toIntOrNull()`, and for lists `firstOrNull()`, `getOrNull(i)` and `filterNotNull()`.

Lists can be nullable in two ways: `List<String?>` holds items that may be null, while `List<String>?` is a list that may itself be missing.

`lateinit var` declares a non-null variable that gets its value a little later instead of straight away (common in test setup). Reading it before it's set fails with an error.
takeaways: `T` can never be null; `T?` may be, and the compiler checks you handle it
`?.` safe call, `?:` Elvis fallback, `?.let` runs code only for non-null values
After a null check, smart casts let you use the value directly
`!!` crashes on null; avoid it
pitfalls: Sprinkling `!!` to silence the compiler instead of handling the null case.

quiz.q: What is the type of s?.length when s is String??
quiz.explain: A safe call can short-circuit to null, so the result type is nullable.

concepts.name: Lists, sets and maps
concepts.summary: Keep groups of values in lists, sets and maps, read-only or changeable, and read, loop over and update them.
concepts.why: Almost all program data lives in collections, and Kotlin's split between read-only and changeable ones prevents accidental changes.
concepts.body:
A **collection** holds a group of values. Kotlin has three main kinds:

- A **list** keeps items in order and allows repeats: `listOf("pen", "ink", "pen")`.
- A **set** keeps only unique items: `setOf(1, 2, 2)` holds just 1 and 2.
- A **map** stores **key-value pairs**: you look up a value by its key, like a word in a dictionary. `mapOf("Ada" to 36, "Bo" to 20)`; `"Ada" to 36` makes one pair.

Each comes in two versions. `listOf`, `setOf` and `mapOf` give **read-only** collections: you can look but not add or remove. `mutableListOf`, `mutableSetOf` and `mutableMapOf` give mutable ones with `add`, `remove`, `clear` and so on. Prefer read-only unless you need changes. Read-only means *you* can't change it through that name; it doesn't promise that no other part of the program can.

Reading values:

- Lists: `list[0]` is the first item. The position is the **index**, and counting starts at 0 (**zero-based indexing**). Also `size`, `first()`, `last()`, `indexOf(x)` and `x in list`. `list.getOrNull(5)` gives null instead of crashing when there's no item at index 5.
- Maps: `map["Ada"]` gives the value, or null (no value) when the key is missing. On a mutable map, `map["Bo"] = 21` sets a value, and `getOrPut(key) { 0 }` adds one (here 0) only if the key is missing.
- Sets: `x in set` checks membership; `add` returns `false` if the item was already there.

Looping: `for (x in list)` visits each item, and `for ((name, age) in map)` visits each pair.

`list + 4` makes a *new* list with 4 added; on a mutable list, `+=` adds in place. Sets and maps remember the order in which items were added.

An **array** (`arrayOf(1, 2)`, `intArrayOf(1, 2)`) is a fixed-size group of values, used mainly for speed and when working with Java code. Prefer lists in everyday code. `List(4) { it * it }` builds a list by working out each item from its index `it`.
concepts.code:
fun main() {
    val nums = listOf(3, 1, 2)
    // nums.add(4)                     // compile error: List is read-only
    println(nums[0] + nums.last())     // 5
    println(nums.getOrNull(10))        // null
    println(2 in nums)                 // true

    val todo = mutableListOf("write")
    todo += "test"
    todo.add(0, "plan")
    println(todo)                      // [plan, write, test]

    val tags = mutableSetOf("kotlin", "jvm")
    println(tags.add("kotlin"))        // false: already present

    val ages = mutableMapOf("Ada" to 36)
    ages["Linus"] = 28
    println(ages["Grace"])             // null
    println(ages.getOrPut("Grace") { 85 }) // 85
    for ((name, age) in ages) print("$name=$age ") // Ada=36 Linus=28 Grace=85
    println()
    println(List(4) { it * it })       // [0, 1, 4, 9]
}
takeaways: `listOf`/`setOf`/`mapOf` are read-only; the `mutable...` versions allow changes
`map[key]` gives null for a missing key
Sets and maps keep the order items were added
Prefer read-only collections unless you really need to change them
pitfalls: Assuming a read-only `List` can never change: if another part of the program holds it as a `MutableList`, it still can.

quiz.q: What does mapOf("a" to 1)["b"] return?
quiz.explain: The indexing operator on Map returns V?, null when the key is missing.

concepts.name: Classes and properties
concepts.summary: Design your own types: classes with a primary constructor, properties, init checks, computed properties and visibility modifiers.
concepts.why: Every real program describes its world (accounts, orders, game pieces) as classes, and Kotlin lets you declare them in very little code.
concepts.body:
A **class** is a blueprint for your own kind of value. An `Account` class can say that every account has an owner and a balance, and that money can be deposited. Each actual account made from it is an **object**, also called an **instance** of the class.

```kotlin
class Account(val owner: String, var balance: Double = 0.0)
val acc = Account("Ada")     // create an object
println(acc.owner)           // Ada
```

The brackets after the class name are the **primary constructor**: the inputs needed to create an object. Writing `val` or `var` in front of an input makes it a **property**, a named value stored in every object and read with a dot (`acc.owner`). Without `val` or `var`, the input is only available while the object is being set up.

Functions written inside a class are its **methods**. They run on one object and can use its properties directly: `fun deposit(amount: Double) { balance += amount }`.

Setup code goes in an `init { }` block, which runs when an object is created. It's the place for checking inputs (**validation**): `require(owner.isNotBlank()) { "owner required" }` stops with an error if the check fails.

A **computed property** works out its value each time it's read: `val isEmpty get() = balance == 0.0`. A custom setter can adjust a value as it's stored: `var name = "" set(value) { field = value.trim() }`, where `field` is the stored value itself.

**Visibility modifiers** control who can use a member: `public` (everyone, the default), `private` (only inside the class), `protected` (also classes built on this one, covered later) and `internal` (only within the same module: the set of files compiled together). `private set` lets everyone read a property but only the class change it.

Every class automatically gets `toString()` (text for printing) and `equals()` (comparison). By default they print an unhelpful code and call two objects equal only if they are the very same object; data classes (next lesson) generate better versions.

Two Kotlin rules to remember: no other class can build on yours unless you mark it `open`, and there's no `static` keyword. Shared helpers go at the top level of a file or in a `companion object` (covered at the Practical level).
takeaways: `val`/`var` inputs of the primary constructor become properties
`init` blocks check inputs; `require()` stops with an error when a check fails
Custom `get()`/`set()` compute or adjust values; `field` is the stored value
No class can build on yours unless you mark it `open`
pitfalls: Leaving out `val` in `class P(name: String)` and then trying to read `p.name`: without `val` or `var` it isn't a property.

quiz.q: What does class P(name: String) (no val or var) give you?
options: A constructor input usable only while the object is set up, not a property
A private property name usable in methods
quiz.explain: Without val or var, the input isn't stored as a property; it's only available in init blocks and property initial values.

concepts.name: Data classes
concepts.summary: Hold plain data in data classes, which get equals, hashCode, toString, copy and destructuring for free.
concepts.why: Data classes are the standard Kotlin way to hold plain data, such as a user record or a reply from a server, in one line.
concepts.body:
Many classes just hold data: a user with a name and an age, a point with x and y. Mark such a class `data` and Kotlin writes the routine code you'd otherwise type by hand (that repetitive code is called **boilerplate**):

```kotlin
data class User(val name: String, val age: Int)
```

Based on the properties in the primary constructor, you get:

- `equals`: two users with the same name and age are equal (`==` is true), so they work in sets and as map keys.
- **hashCode**: a number summarising the values, which sets and maps use to find items quickly.
- `toString`: prints `User(name=Ada, age=36)`.
- `copy(age = 37)`: a new object with one value changed, leaving the original as it was. That's how you "change" **immutable** data, data that can't change after creation.
- Destructuring: `val (name, age) = user` unpacks the properties into two variables.

`==` compares contents; `===` asks whether two names refer to the very same object.

Rules: the primary constructor needs at least one `val` or `var` property, and a data class can't be `open` or `abstract`. Only properties in the primary constructor take part in `equals` and `toString`; properties declared in the class body are ignored.

Use `val` properties so objects can't change after creation. Note that `copy` is shallow: a mutable list inside is shared between the copy and the original.

Destructuring also works in loops: `for ((name, age) in users)`. Write `_` for parts you don't need.

Kotlin's ready-made `Pair` and `Triple` are data classes too, but a named data class almost always reads better. For wrapping a single value cheaply, see value classes at the Expert level.
concepts.code:
data class User(val name: String, val age: Int, val tags: List<String> = emptyList())

fun main() {
    val a = User("Ada", 36)
    val b = User("Ada", 36)
    println(a == b)              // true  (same values)
    println(a === b)             // false (two separate objects)
    println(a)                   // User(name=Ada, age=36, tags=[])

    val older = a.copy(age = 37)
    println("${a.age} ${older.age}") // 36 37

    val (name, age) = older
    println("$name is $age")     // Ada is 37

    val users = setOf(a, b, older)
    println(users.size)          // 2 (a and b are equal, so the set keeps one)

    for ((n, _) in listOf(User("Bo", 20), User("Cy", 30))) print("$n ") // Bo Cy
}
takeaways: `data` generates equals, hashCode, toString, copy and destructuring
Only primary-constructor properties count
`copy(...)` makes a changed copy; it is shallow
Destructure with `val (a, b) = obj`
pitfalls: Declaring a property in the class body and expecting it to be part of equals.

quiz.q: For data class P(val x: Int) { var note = "" }, are P(1).apply { note = "a" } and P(1) equal?
quiz.explain: equals uses only primary constructor properties, so note is ignored.

concepts.name: Lambdas and higher-order functions
concepts.summary: Pass functions as values with lambdas, function types, it, trailing lambda syntax and function references.
concepts.why: Lambdas power Kotlin's collection functions, coroutines and almost every modern Kotlin library.
concepts.body:
In Kotlin, functions are values: you can store them in variables and pass them to other functions. A function that takes or returns another function is a **higher-order function**. The type of a function is written as a **function type**, such as `(Int, Int) -> Int` (two Ints in, an Int out) or `() -> Unit`; a nullable one is `((String) -> Unit)?`.

A **lambda** is a function without a name, written in braces: `{ a: Int, b: Int -> a + b }`. Conventions that make Kotlin code read so smoothly:

- If a lambda has exactly one parameter, you can omit it and use `it`: `list.filter { it > 0 }`.
- **Trailing lambdas**: if a function's last parameter is a function, pass the lambda outside the parentheses: `repeat(3) { println(it) }`. If it's the only argument, drop the parentheses entirely.
- The **last expression** in a lambda is its return value; a bare `return` inside a lambda passed to `forEach` (and other inline functions, see the Expert level) returns from the whole surrounding function, so use a label (`return@forEach`) to leave just the lambda.
- Unused parameters are written `_`.

**Function references** pass existing functions as values: `::isEven`, `String::length`, `user::greet`, `::User` (a constructor).

A lambda can use, and even change, the `var`s of the function around it; using an outside variable like this is called **capturing** it.

Anonymous functions (`fun(x: Int): Int { return x * 2 }`) allow normal `return` semantics when you need them.

Kotlin's own built-in functions are full of these: `map`, `filter`, `sortedBy`, `let`, `apply`, `use`, `lazy`, `thread { }`.
takeaways: Function types: (A, B) -> R; lambdas: { a, b -> ... }
it names a single parameter; trailing lambdas go outside parentheses
::name creates function references
Use return@label to return from a lambda
pitfalls: Writing return inside a forEach lambda and unintentionally returning from the whole function.

quiz.q: In list.forEach { if (it == 2) return }, inside fun main(), what does return do?
quiz.explain: forEach is inline, so a bare return is a non-local return from the enclosing function.

concepts.name: Collection operations
concepts.summary: Transform data with map, filter, groupBy, associate, fold, sortedBy, partition, zip and sequences.
concepts.why: Most everyday logic is reshaping data, and the collection functions turn loops into clear step-by-step chains.
concepts.body:
Kotlin comes with a rich set of functions on collections, most taking a lambda. Each returns a **new** collection (or a single value) and leaves the original alone. The core ones:

- `map { }` turns each element into something else: `listOf(1, 2).map { it * 10 }` gives `[10, 20]`.
- `filter { }` keeps only the elements for which the lambda returns `true`.
- `first { }` gives the first element that matches; `any { }` and `all { }` ask whether at least one, or every, element matches.
- `sumOf { }` adds up a number taken from each element.
- `maxByOrNull { }` finds the element with the biggest value, or `null` if the list is empty.
- `sortedBy { }` returns a copy sorted by the value the lambda picks.
- `groupBy { }` builds a map from each key to the list of elements with that key (`Map<K, List<T>>`).
- `fold(start) { acc, x -> }` walks the list carrying a running result, `acc`, that begins as `start`.

Many more follow the same patterns, and the official docs list them all. The example also uses `mapValues` (changes each value of a map), `partition` (splits a list into the matching and the non-matching elements), `associateBy` (a map from a key to each element) and `chunked` (cuts a list into pieces of a fixed size).

Collection operations are **eager**: each step runs straight away and builds a complete in-between list. For long chains over large data, or infinite data, use a **sequence**: `list.asSequence().filter { }.map { }.take(10).toList()`. A sequence is **lazy**: it passes elements through the steps one at a time, only as they're needed, and stops as soon as it can.

`first()` stops the program with an error (an **exception**) when nothing matches; `firstOrNull()` returns `null` instead. Prefer `sumOf { it.price }` over `map { it.price }.sum()`. Readability first: a short `for` loop is fine when a chain would get clever.
takeaways: map/filter/groupBy/fold build new collections
Prefer firstOrNull, maxByOrNull to avoid exceptions on empty input
Collection operations are eager; asSequence() makes them lazy
Use sumOf, associateBy, partition instead of manual loops
pitfalls: Chaining many operations over huge lists without asSequence(), creating large intermediate lists.

quiz.q: What does listOf(1, 2, 3, 4).partition { it % 2 == 0 } return?
quiz.explain: partition returns a Pair whose first list holds the items that match the condition.

concepts.name: Inheritance and interfaces
concepts.summary: Extend open classes, override members, write abstract classes and implement interfaces with default methods.
concepts.why: Interfaces and controlled inheritance structure larger programs, and **frameworks** such as Android's (ready-made code that calls yours) rely on them.
concepts.body:
A class can build on another class, getting all its properties and methods and adding or changing some. This is **inheritance**: the new class is a **subclass**, the original its **base class** (or superclass). Kotlin classes are *final* by default, meaning they can't be built on, so mark a class `open` to allow it, and mark `open` each member that subclasses may replace. A subclass replaces (**overrides**) such a member with `override`, which stays open unless written `final override`.

```kotlin
open class Animal(val name: String) { open fun sound() = "..." }
class Dog(name: String) : Animal(name) { override fun sound() = "Woof" }
```

The superclass constructor is called in the header: `: Animal(name)`. Call the parent implementation with `super.sound()`.

An **abstract class** can't be used to create objects directly. It may declare `abstract` members, with no body, that subclasses must fill in.

An **interface** is a list of properties and methods that a class promises to provide. It may give **default implementations** (bodies used unless overridden), and it can declare properties but not store values in them. A class extends at most one class but implements any number of interfaces, listed after the colon: `class Robot : Machine(), Speaker, Walker`. If two interfaces provide the same default method, you must override it and can pick one with `super<Speaker>.speak()`.

**Type checks**: `is` checks and smart-casts (`if (a is Dog) a.fetch()`), `as` converts (casts) to a more specific type and throws an error if the value isn't that type; `as?` gives null instead.

**Delegation** (`class Logger(w: Writer) : Writer by w`) implements an interface by forwarding to another object, a concise alternative to inheritance (Advanced lesson).

Kotlin's closed-by-default design nudges you towards composition: holding a helper object instead of extending a class. Frameworks such as Spring, which need to extend your classes, use the `kotlin-spring` compiler plugin to open them automatically.
takeaways: Classes and members are final unless marked open
override is required and explicit; call super.member()
Interfaces can have default methods but no state
is smart-casts; as? casts safely to null
pitfalls: Forgetting open on the base class and getting 'This type is final, so it cannot be inherited from'.

quiz.q: Why does class B : A() fail to compile when A is declared class A?
options: A is final by default; it must be marked open
quiz.explain: Kotlin classes are final unless explicitly declared open.

concepts.name: Objects and companion objects
concepts.summary: Create singletons with object declarations, class-level members with companion objects, and one-off objects with object expressions.
concepts.why: Kotlin has no static keyword; objects and companions are how you write singletons, factories and constants.
concepts.body:
An **object declaration** defines a class and its one and only instance at once. A class with exactly one instance is a **singleton**. Kotlin creates it the first time it's used, and does so safely even if several parts of the program running at the same time touch it at once:

```kotlin
object Registry { val items = mutableListOf<String>() }
Registry.items.add("a")
```

Objects can implement interfaces and extend classes, which makes them handy for objects that hold no data of their own, such as a sorting rule (a `Comparator`).

A **companion object** lives inside a class and holds members that belong to the class itself rather than to each instance; you call them through the class name:

```kotlin
class User private constructor(val name: String) {
    companion object { fun of(raw: String) = User(raw.trim()) }
}
User.of(" Ada ")
```

Typical uses: **factory functions** (functions that create instances, often paired with a private constructor so they're the only way in), constants (`const val MAX = 10`) and loggers. A companion can have a name and implement interfaces. For Java code calling yours, add the **annotation** `@JvmStatic` or `@JvmField` (a tag starting with `@` that the compiler reads) to get Java-style static members.

An **object expression** creates a one-off object of an unnamed class right where it's written:

```kotlin
val cmp = object : Comparator<String> { override fun compare(a: String, b: String) = a.length - b.length }
```

**Data objects** (`data object Loading`) give a singleton a nice `toString`, which is useful in sealed hierarchies.

Remember that a singleton is shared by the whole program. Keep singletons free of changing data, or pass the objects a class needs into its constructor instead of reaching for a global object everywhere, which makes testing hard.
takeaways: object Name declares a lazily created, thread-safe singleton
companion object holds class-level members such as factories and constants
object : Interface { } creates anonymous instances
Use @JvmStatic for static access from Java
pitfalls: Keeping changing data in an object declaration, so it carries over from one test to the next.

quiz.q: How do you call a companion object function create() defined in class Foo?
quiz.explain: Companion members are accessed through the class name.

concepts.name: Enums and sealed hierarchies
concepts.summary: Model fixed sets of values with enum classes and closed type hierarchies with sealed classes and exhaustive when.
concepts.why: Sealed types make impossible states impossible to write down, and let the compiler check that every possibility is handled.
concepts.body:
An **enum** class (short for enumeration) defines a type with a fixed set of named values. Each constant can carry properties and the enum can have methods:

```kotlin
enum class Level(val weight: Int) { LOW(1), MEDIUM(5), HIGH(10) }
```

Enums provide `name`, `ordinal` (the position in the list), `entries` (all values, preferred over the older `values()`), and `valueOf("HIGH")`.

A **sealed class** or **sealed interface** lists its possible subclasses up front (they must be declared in the same module and package), so the compiler knows the full list. Unlike enums, each subtype can be a different class with its own data and many instances:

```kotlin
sealed interface Result {
    data class Ok(val value: String) : Result
    data class Error(val message: String, val code: Int) : Result
    data object Loading : Result
}
```

The payoff is an **exhaustive `when`**: when every subtype is covered, no `else` branch is needed, and adding a new subtype later produces compile errors at every `when` that doesn't handle it. This is far safer than an `else` that silently swallows new subtypes.

Inside each branch the value is smart-cast, so you can access `result.value` or `result.message` directly. Kotlin 2.2 also allows guard conditions: `is Result.Error if result.code >= 500 -> ...`.

Use enums for simple labels, and sealed hierarchies for states, events, replies from other programs and the possible outcomes of an operation.
takeaways: enum class for fixed constants with properties; use entries to list them
Sealed classes/interfaces fix the set of subtypes at compile time
when over a sealed type is exhaustive without else
Avoid else on sealed when: you lose compile errors for new cases
pitfalls: Adding an else branch to a sealed when, so new subtypes are silently unhandled.

quiz.q: What happens when you add a new subtype to a sealed interface that is matched in a when without else?
options: Compile errors where the when is used as an expression and becomes non-exhaustive
A runtime exception when the new case appears
The when picks the first branch
quiz.explain: The compiler knows the full set of subtypes, so non-exhaustive when expressions stop compiling.

concepts.name: Extension functions
concepts.summary: Add functions and properties to existing types without inheritance, including nullable receivers.
concepts.why: Extensions are how Kotlin's built-in functions and Android's KTX add handy functions to existing classes, and how you write readable helpers.
concepts.body:
An **extension function** adds a function to an existing type, even one you don't own, such as `String` or a Java class:

```kotlin
fun String.isPalindrome(): Boolean = this == reversed()
"level".isPalindrome()   // true
```

Inside, `this` refers to the **receiver** object (and can be omitted). **Extension properties** work similarly but can't store a value (they have no `field`): `val String.wordCount get() = split(" ").size`.

Under the hood, an extension compiles to an ordinary top-level function that takes the receiver as its first parameter. Consequences:

- Extensions can't access `private` or `protected` members.
- They're chosen by the declared type of the variable when the code is compiled, not by the actual object while the program runs. So, unlike overridden methods, they don't adapt to subclasses.
- A method of the class with the same name and parameters always wins over an extension.
- If declared in another file's package, they must be imported where used.

Extensions on **nullable receivers** can be called on null: `fun String?.orDash() = this ?: "-"`. That's how the standard library's `isNullOrEmpty()` works.

One extension can work for many types: `fun <T> List<T>.second() = this[1]` works on a list of anything (`T` stands for any type; see Generics).

Good uses: small helpers that make code read naturally, wrappers that make Java libraries feel like Kotlin, and utility code that would otherwise sit in separate helper classes. Avoid putting core domain behavior in scattered extensions where readers won't find it.
concepts.code:
fun String.isPalindrome(): Boolean = this == reversed()

val String.wordCount: Int
    get() = split(" ").count { it.isNotBlank() }

fun String?.orDash(): String = if (isNullOrBlank()) "-" else this

fun <T> List<T>.secondOrNull(): T? = getOrNull(1)

open class Animal
class Dog : Animal()
fun Animal.kind() = "animal"
fun Dog.kind() = "dog"

fun main() {
    println("level".isPalindrome())         // true
    println("hello  big world".wordCount)   // 3
    val missing: String? = null
    println(missing.orDash())               // -
    println(listOf(1, 2, 3).secondOrNull()) // 2

    val pet: Animal = Dog()
    println(pet.kind())                     // animal (static resolution!)
}
takeaways: fun Type.name() adds functions callable with dot syntax
this is the receiver; private members are not accessible
Extensions are chosen by the declared type, not the actual object
Nullable receivers let you call extensions on null
pitfalls: Expecting an extension on a subclass to override one on the base class.

quiz.q: val a: Animal = Dog(); a.kind() with extensions on both Animal and Dog calls which?
quiz.explain: Extensions are chosen by the declared type of the variable, which is Animal.

concepts.name: Scope functions: let, apply, also, run, with
concepts.summary: Choose between let, run, with, apply and also by how they refer to the object and what they return.
concepts.why: Scope functions appear in nearly all Kotlin code; picking the right one keeps it readable.
concepts.body:
The five **scope functions** run a block of code in the context of an object. They differ in two ways: how the block refers to the object (`it` or `this`), and what the call returns (the block's result or the object itself).

- `let`: object as `it`, returns the block result. Typical: `value?.let { use(it) }` to run code only for non-null values, or transforming a value.
- `run`: object as `this`, returns the block result. Computing something from an object's members.
- `with(obj) { }`: like `run` but not an extension; "with this object, do...".
- `apply`: object as `this`, returns **the object**. Configuring a newly created object: `Paint().apply { color = RED; width = 2f }`.
- `also`: object as `it`, returns **the object**. Extra actions in a chain (**side effects**): logging, validation, adding to a list.

Rules of thumb: `apply` for configuration, `also` for "and also do this", `let` for null checks and mapping, `run`/`with` for grouping calls on one object.

Don't nest them deeply or chain many; when `it` and `this` become ambiguous, a local variable is clearer. `takeIf { cond }` and `takeUnless` return the object or null and pair nicely with `?.let`.
concepts.code:
data class Config(var host: String = "", var port: Int = 0, var debug: Boolean = false)

fun main() {
    val cfg = Config().apply {          // configure, returns the object
        host = "localhost"
        port = 8080
    }
    println(cfg)                        // Config(host=localhost, port=8080, debug=false)

    val url = cfg.run { "http://$host:$port" }       // compute from members
    println(url)                        // http://localhost:8080

    val log = mutableListOf<String>()
    val users = listOf("ada", "bo")
        .also { log += "loaded ${it.size}" }         // side effect, passes list on
        .map { it.replaceFirstChar(Char::uppercase) }
    println("$users $log")              // [Ada, Bo] [loaded 2]

    val input: String? = " 42 "
    val n = input?.trim()?.toIntOrNull()?.let { it * 2 } ?: 0
    println(n)                          // 84
    val port = with(cfg) { if (debug) 9000 else port }
    println(port)                       // 8080
    println(cfg.port.takeIf { it > 1024 })           // 8080
}
takeaways: let/also use it; run/with/apply use this
apply and also return the object; let, run and with return the block result
apply to configure, also for side effects, let for null checks
Prefer a named variable over deeply nested scope functions
pitfalls: Using apply when you meant let, and getting the object instead of the computed value.

quiz.q: What does "abc".also { it.uppercase() } return?
quiz.explain: also returns the receiver object unchanged; the block's result is discarded.

concepts.name: Exceptions and error handling
concepts.summary: Throw and catch exceptions, use try as an expression, require/check preconditions, and model failures with Result.
concepts.why: Choosing between exceptions, nullable returns and Result types shapes robust Kotlin APIs.
concepts.body:
When something goes wrong while a program runs, Kotlin code throws an **exception**: an error object that stops normal execution until some code catches it with `try`/`catch` (**exception handling**). If nothing catches it, the program stops and prints the error. Unlike Java, Kotlin has no **checked exceptions**: the compiler never forces you to catch or declare them (`@Throws` exists only for Java code calling yours).

`try` is an **expression**:

```kotlin
val n = try { s.toInt() } catch (e: NumberFormatException) { 0 }
```

`throw` is an expression of type `Nothing` (a type meaning "never finishes normally"), so it can be used after the Elvis operator: `val user = find(id) ?: throw NotFoundException(id)`. `finally` runs regardless. For things that must be closed after use, such as open files, `use { }` closes them automatically, even after an error.

Preconditions from the standard library:

- `require(cond) { "message" }` throws `IllegalArgumentException` for bad arguments.
- `check(cond)` throws `IllegalStateException` for bad state.
- `requireNotNull(x)` / `checkNotNull(x)` return the non-null value; `error("msg")` throws `IllegalStateException`.

Alternatives to throwing:

- Return `null` for "not found" or "can't parse" (`toIntOrNull`).
- Return a sealed result type for domain errors with data.
- `runCatching { }` wraps a block into `Result<T>`, with `getOrNull()`, `getOrElse { }`, `onFailure`, `map`. Note it catches everything, including the signal coroutines use to stop (see Coroutines), so avoid it around suspending code.

Use exceptions for programming errors and truly exceptional failures; use types for expected outcomes callers must handle.
takeaways: No checked exceptions; try and throw are expressions
require for arguments, check for state, error() to fail
use { } closes resources
Return null, sealed results or Result for expected failures
pitfalls: Wrapping coroutine code in runCatching, which swallows the signal that tells a coroutine to stop.

quiz.q: Which exception does require(x > 0) throw when x is 0?
quiz.explain: require is for argument checks and throws IllegalArgumentException; check throws IllegalStateException.

concepts.name: Generics and variance
concepts.summary: Write generic classes and functions with bounds, declaration-site variance (in/out), star projections and reified type parameters.
concepts.why: Variance and reified generics explain the declarations of library functions and let you write reusable code that the compiler can still check.
concepts.body:
**Generics** let a class or function work with a type chosen by whoever uses it: `class Box<T>(val value: T)` can hold any type `T`, and `fun <T> List<T>.second(): T` works on any list. **Upper bounds** restrict type arguments: `fun <T : Comparable<T>> maxOf(a: T, b: T)`; several bounds use `where T : A, T : B`.

**Variance** decides when a `Box<Cat>` may be used as a `Box<Animal>`. Kotlin uses **declaration-site variance**:

- `out T` (**covariant**): the class only produces `T`. Kotlin's `List<out E>` is read-only, so a `List<String>` is a `List<Any>`.
- `in T` (**contravariant**): the class only consumes `T`, like `Comparable<in T>`. A `Comparator<Any>` can compare strings.
- No modifier: **invariant**. `MutableList<String>` is not a `MutableList<Any>`, otherwise you could add an `Int` to it.

The compiler enforces that `out` types appear only in output positions and `in` types only in inputs. **Use-site variance** (`fun copy(from: Array<out Any>, to: Array<Any>)`) handles classes that aren't variant themselves. A **star projection** `List<*>` means "a list of some unknown type": safe to read as `Any?`, not to write.

On the JVM, type arguments are removed (**erased**) after compiling, so while running `x is List<String>` can't be checked. **Reified** type parameters on `inline` functions (whose code is copied into every caller; see the Expert level) keep the type: `inline fun <reified T> Any.isA() = this is T`. That's how `filterIsInstance<T>()` works.
takeaways: out = producer (covariant), in = consumer (contravariant)
List<out E> is covariant; MutableList<E> is invariant
Generics are erased on the JVM; inline + reified keeps the type
List<*> reads as Any? but can't be written to

quiz.q: Why can a List<String> be assigned to List<Any> but a MutableList<String> not to MutableList<Any>?
options: List is declared with out E (read-only); MutableList is invariant because it accepts writes
quiz.explain: Allowing it for MutableList would let you add non-String values into a list of strings.

concepts.name: Coroutines and suspend functions
concepts.summary: Write code that waits without blocking, as plain top-to-bottom steps, with suspend functions, launch, async/await and runBlocking.
concepts.why: Coroutines are Kotlin's standard way to do several things at once on Android and on servers, replacing tangled callbacks and blocked threads.
concepts.body:
Programs often wait: for a file, a reply over the network, a timer. A **thread** is one sequence of steps running inside a program, and a program can run several at once. A thread that just sits waiting (**blocking**) is wasted.

A **coroutine** is a lightweight task that can pause, or **suspend**, while it waits for input/output (**I/O**) or a delay, handing its thread to other work, and resume later. Thousands of coroutines can share a few threads. Code that starts slow work and deals with the result later is called **asynchronous**; coroutines let you write it as plain top-to-bottom steps instead of **callbacks** (functions handed over to be called later).

The language provides `suspend` functions; the library `kotlinx.coroutines` (add `org.jetbrains.kotlinx:kotlinx-coroutines-core` to your Gradle build) provides the tools for starting and managing coroutines.

- A `suspend fun` can call other suspending functions such as `delay(100)`. It can only be called from another suspend function or a coroutine.
- `runBlocking { }` starts a coroutine and blocks the current thread until it finishes: for `main` functions and tests only.
- `launch { }` starts a coroutine for work whose result you don't need and returns a `Job` (`join()` waits for it).
- `async { }` starts a coroutine that computes a value and returns a `Deferred<T>`; `await()` suspends until the result is ready.
- `coroutineScope { }` groups child coroutines in a suspend function and waits for all of them.

Code inside a coroutine reads **sequentially**: `val user = fetchUser(); val orders = fetchOrders(user)`. To run independent calls at the same time (**concurrency**), start both with `async` and then `await` both.

Use `delay` instead of `Thread.sleep` inside coroutines: `sleep` blocks the thread. For code that blocks a thread, such as older database libraries or file reading, wrap it in `withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { }` (next lesson).

Frameworks provide scopes for you: `viewModelScope` and `lifecycleScope` on Android, suspend handlers in Ktor and Spring WebFlux.
takeaways: suspend functions pause without blocking their thread
launch for fire-and-forget Jobs, async/await for results
Start several async calls before awaiting to run them concurrently
runBlocking only in main and tests; use delay, not Thread.sleep
pitfalls: Calling Thread.sleep or blocking I/O inside a coroutine on a limited dispatcher, starving other coroutines.

quiz.q: val a = async { f() }.await(); val b = async { g() }.await() with each taking 1 s. Total time?
quiz.explain: Each await happens right after its async, so the calls run one after another.

concepts.name: Structured concurrency and cancellation
concepts.summary: Understand coroutine scopes, parent-child jobs, dispatchers, withContext, cancellation and exception propagation.
concepts.why: Structured concurrency is what makes coroutines safe: no leaked work, predictable cancellation and error handling.
concepts.body:
**Structured concurrency** means every coroutine runs inside a `CoroutineScope`, and a parent doesn't complete until all its children do. If a child fails, the parent is cancelled along with its other children, and the exception propagates up. If the parent is cancelled, all children are cancelled. Nothing leaks.

`coroutineScope { }` creates such a scope inside a suspend function. `supervisorScope { }` (or a `SupervisorJob`) changes the rule so one child's failure doesn't cancel its siblings, useful for independent tasks such as per-connection handlers.

**Dispatchers** decide which threads run a coroutine:

- `Dispatchers.Default`: work that keeps the processor busy (**CPU-bound**), with as many threads as the processor has cores.
- `Dispatchers.IO`: blocking I/O, with a larger set of threads (64 by default).
- `Dispatchers.Main`: the thread that draws the app's screen (the **main thread**) on Android and desktop.
- Switch with `withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { blockingCall() }`, which suspends until the block finishes and returns its result.

**Cancellation** is cooperative. Suspending functions from kotlinx.coroutines (`delay`, `withContext`, channel operations) check for cancellation and throw `CancellationException`. CPU loops must check `isActive` or call `ensureActive()` / `yield()`. Use `withTimeout(ms)` or `withTimeoutOrNull` for time limits (**timeouts**). Never swallow `CancellationException`: rethrow it if you catch `Exception` broadly.

Avoid `GlobalScope`: it breaks structure. Long-lived components should own a scope (`CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.Default)`) and cancel it when they shut down.
takeaways: Children run inside their parent's scope; the parent waits for all of them
A failing child cancels its siblings unless you use supervisorScope
withContext(Dispatchers.IO) for blocking calls, Default for CPU work
Cancellation is cooperative; never swallow CancellationException
pitfalls: Launching work in GlobalScope, so it outlives the request or screen that started it.

quiz.q: In coroutineScope { launch { A } ; launch { B fails } }, what happens to A?
options: A is cancelled and the exception propagates from coroutineScope
A keeps running and the error is ignored
quiz.explain: In a regular scope a child failure cancels the parent and all its other children.

concepts.name: Flows
concepts.summary: Model values that arrive over time with Flow: builders, operators, collection, StateFlow and SharedFlow.
concepts.why: Flows are the standard Kotlin way to handle values that keep coming: changes from a database, what's on screen, live messages from a server, and long lists loaded page by page.
concepts.body:
A **Flow** (`Flow<T>`) is a **stream** of values that arrive one by one over time, built on coroutines. Where a `suspend` function returns one value, a flow emits many over time.

```kotlin
val numbers: Flow<Int> = flow { for (i in 1..3) { delay(100); emit(i) } }
```

Flows are **cold**: the block doesn't run until someone calls a **terminal operator** like `collect { }`, `toList()`, `first()` or `fold`, and each collector gets its own execution.

Intermediate operators look like collection operations but are lazy and suspend-friendly: `map`, `filter`, `take`, `transform`, `onEach`, `distinctUntilChanged`, `debounce`, `combine`, `zip`, `flatMapLatest`. `catch { }` handles upstream errors; `onCompletion` runs at the end.

Context: a flow runs in the collector's coroutine. To move the steps before it (upstream) to another dispatcher, use `flowOn(Dispatchers.IO)`; never call `withContext` around `emit`. `buffer()` and `conflate()` decouple slow collectors from fast producers.

**Hot flows** exist independently of collectors:

- `StateFlow<T>` always holds a current value (`.value`), emits only distinct updates, and new collectors get the latest value immediately. It's the standard holder for what an app's screen shows (`MutableStateFlow` inside, exposed as read-only `StateFlow`).
- `SharedFlow<T>` broadcasts events to all current subscribers, with configurable replay.

Convert cold to hot with `stateIn` / `shareIn` in a scope.
takeaways: flow { emit(x) } is cold: it runs per collector on collect
Operators like map/filter/catch are lazy and suspend-friendly
flowOn changes the upstream dispatcher; don't use withContext around emit
StateFlow holds current state; SharedFlow broadcasts events
pitfalls: Collecting a flow in a scope that is never cancelled, leaking a collector forever.

quiz.q: When does the block of a cold flow { } run?
options: Once, on first collection, then values are cached
Each time a terminal operator such as collect is called
quiz.explain: Cold flows run their producer separately for every collector.

concepts.name: Delegation and delegated properties
concepts.summary: Implement interfaces by delegation with by, and reuse property logic with lazy, observable, map-backed and custom delegates.
concepts.why: Delegation replaces much inheritance and boilerplate, and lazy initialization is used everywhere.
concepts.body:
**Class delegation** implements an interface by handing (**delegating**) every call to another object:

```kotlin
class LoggingList<T>(private val inner: MutableList<T>) : MutableList<T> by inner {
    override fun add(element: T): Boolean { println("add $element"); return inner.add(element) }
}
```

The compiler generates all the forwarding methods; you override only what you want to change. This is "composition over inheritance" (holding a helper object instead of extending a class) without the boilerplate.

**Delegated properties** hand a property's get/set logic to a delegate object: `val x: T by delegate`. Standard delegates:

- `by lazy { ... }`: computed on first access, then remembered (**cached**). This **lazy** start is safe even when several threads read it at once (`LazyThreadSafetyMode.SYNCHRONIZED`).
- `by Delegates.observable(initial) { prop, old, new -> }`: runs a function you supply after each change.
- `by Delegates.vetoable(initial) { _, old, new -> condition }`: rejects changes that fail the check.
- `by map`: reads properties from a `Map<String, Any?>` by name, handy for dynamic data.
- `by ::otherProperty`: delegates to another property (for renames/deprecations).

You can write your own delegate: any object with `operator fun getValue(thisRef, property)` (and `setValue` for `var`), or implement `ReadOnlyProperty` / `ReadWriteProperty`. The `property.name` lets one delegate class serve many properties, as in preference or settings wrappers.

Android's `by viewModels()` and Compose's `by remember { mutableStateOf() }` are delegated properties too.
takeaways: Interface by obj generates forwarding methods; override only what changes
by lazy computes once on first access, thread-safe by default
observable/vetoable react to or veto property changes
Custom delegates implement getValue/setValue

quiz.q: When is the initializer of val x by lazy { compute() } executed?
options: On the first access of x, then the value is cached
quiz.explain: lazy defers computation to the first read and caches the result.

concepts.name: Java interoperability
concepts.summary: Call Java from Kotlin and Kotlin from Java: platform types, getters as properties, SAM conversions and @Jvm annotations.
concepts.why: Most Kotlin code runs alongside Java libraries and frameworks; smooth interop is a key Kotlin strength.
concepts.body:
**Calling Java from Kotlin** mostly just works:

- Java getters and setters (methods named `getX`/`setX` that read and change a value) appear as properties: `user.getName()` / `setName()` become `user.name`.
- Values from Java have **platform types** (`String!`): Kotlin doesn't know whether they can be null, so it lets you treat them as nullable or not, and a wrong guess fails at runtime. Declare the Kotlin type explicitly at the boundary (`val name: String? = javaObj.name`). Nullability annotations (`@Nullable`, JSpecify `@NullMarked`) on the Java side give Kotlin real types.
- **SAM conversion**: a lambda can be passed where Java expects an interface with a single abstract method (SAM), such as `Runnable` or `Comparator`. For Kotlin interfaces, declare them `fun interface` to get the same.
- Java's checked exceptions (ones Java forces callers to handle) don't need to be caught in Kotlin.
- If a Java name is a Kotlin **keyword** (a word with special meaning, such as `when`), wrap it in backticks: ``Mockito.`when`(...)``.

**Calling Kotlin from Java** needs a few annotations:

- Top-level functions in `Utils.kt` appear to Java as **static methods** (methods that belong to a class, not an object) of a class named `UtilsKt`; rename with `@file:JvmName("Utils")`.
- `@JvmStatic` on companion or object members creates real static methods; `@JvmField` exposes a property as a plain Java field (a variable stored directly in the object).
- `@JvmOverloads` generates one Java method per combination of default arguments (**overloads**), because Java has no default arguments.
- `@Throws(IOException::class)` declares checked exceptions for Java callers.

Kotlin collections map to Java's (`List` is `java.util.List`); read-only is a compile-time view only, so Java code can still mutate them.
concepts.code:
import java.util.Optional
import java.util.concurrent.Executors

fun interface Validator { fun validate(s: String): Boolean }   // SAM for Kotlin
object MathUtils {
    @JvmStatic fun twice(x: Int) = x * 2                        // static for Java
    @JvmOverloads fun greet(name: String, greeting: String = "Hi") = "$greeting $name"
}
fun main() {
    val sb = java.lang.StringBuilder()
    sb.append("abc")
    println(sb.length)                       // 3 (Java length() as a property)
    val names = java.util.ArrayList<String>()
    names.add("b"); names.add("a")
    names.sortWith { x, y -> x.compareTo(y) } // lambda -> java.util.Comparator
    println(names)                           // [a, b]
    val env: String? = System.getenv("NOT_SET")  // platform type made explicit
    println(env ?: "unset")                  // unset
    val notBlank = Validator { it.isNotBlank() }
    println(notBlank.validate(" "))          // false
    println(Optional.ofNullable<String>(null).orElse("none")) // none
    val pool = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor()
    println(pool.submit<Int> { MathUtils.twice(21) }.get())  // 42
    pool.shutdown()
}
takeaways: Java getters/setters become Kotlin properties
Platform types (T!) have unknown nullability: declare the type at the boundary
Lambdas convert to Java SAM interfaces; use fun interface in Kotlin
@JvmStatic, @JvmOverloads, @JvmName shape the Java-facing API
pitfalls: Letting a Java method's platform-typed null flow into a non-null Kotlin variable, causing an NPE far from the source.

quiz.q: Java code calls a Kotlin function fun f(a: Int, b: Int = 0). Without annotations, what can Java do?
options: Only call f(a, b) with both arguments
quiz.explain: Default arguments are a Kotlin feature; @JvmOverloads generates the shorter overloads for Java.

concepts.name: Inline functions and value classes
concepts.summary: Know what inline, noinline and crossinline do to lambdas, and wrap values without allocation using value classes.
concepts.why: These features explain why Kotlin's built-in helpers like map and let cost nothing extra, and let you give IDs their own types at no cost.
concepts.body:
Every lambda passed to a normal function becomes an object in memory, a lambda that captures variables creates a new object (a **memory allocation**) on each call, and calling it costs a little time. An **inline function** avoids this: the compiler copies the function body and the lambda's code into each call site.

```kotlin
inline fun <T> measure(block: () -> T): T { val t = System.nanoTime(); return block().also { println(System.nanoTime() - t) } }
```

Effects of inlining:

- No lambda allocation or call overhead; this is why `map`, `filter`, `let`, `use` cost nothing extra.
- **Non-local returns**: a bare `return` inside an inlined lambda returns from the surrounding function.
- **Reified** type parameters become possible because the actual type is known at each call site.

Modifiers on lambda parameters: `noinline` keeps one lambda as an object (so you can store or pass it on); `crossinline` forbids non-local returns, required when the lambda is called from another context such as a nested object or another lambda. Inline only small functions that take lambdas; inlining big bodies bloats bytecode.

A **value class** wraps a single value in a distinct type, usually without creating an extra object:

```kotlin
@JvmInline value class UserId(val raw: Long)
```

At runtime a `UserId` is mostly just a `long`, but the compiler won't let you pass an `OrderId` where a `UserId` is expected. It gets wrapped in a real object (**boxed**) when used as a nullable, generic or interface type. Functions taking value classes get altered (**mangled**) names in the bytecode, which matters for Java code calling them.
takeaways: inline copies the function and lambda bodies to the call site: no allocations
Inlined lambdas allow non-local return and reified types
noinline keeps a lambda as an object; crossinline forbids non-local returns
Value classes give type safety for wrapped values, usually without allocation
pitfalls: Marking large functions without lambda parameters inline, bloating bytecode for no benefit.

quiz.q: Why is crossinline needed when an inline function calls its lambda inside a Runnable?
options: Because a non-local return from inside the Runnable would be impossible
quiz.explain: The lambda runs in a different execution context, so non-local returns must be forbidden.

concepts.name: Type-safe builders and DSLs
concepts.summary: Build Kotlin DSLs (mini-languages for one job) with lambdas with receivers, extension function types and @DslMarker.
concepts.why: Gradle's Kotlin build scripts, Ktor routing, Compose and kotlinx.html are all built this way; understanding it demystifies them.
concepts.body:
